To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) PRAMs can be simulated on MPCs and bounded-degree networks with a small number of steps, (2) the lower bound on the simulation time of PRAMs is Ω((log n)^2/log log n), and (3) the simulation time is Ω(log^2 n) for MPCs and bounded degree networks.
(1) the number of MPC steps needed for simulating PRAMs on MPCs is O(log n) and that (2) the number of steps of bounded-degree networks needed to simulate PRAMs is O((log n)^2).
(i) the MPC model is as powerful as the PRAM model and that (ii) the PRAM model is as powerful (or at least as close to being as powerful) as the model of bounded-degree networks.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: What is the complexity of the deterministic simulation of a PRAM by a MPC or a bounded-degree network?

the question whether the MPC model is a good abstraction for the design of parallel algorithms and with the question how much the MPC model can be simplified without losing the ability to simulate PRAMs efficiently.

the simulation of PRAM on bounded-degree networks is possible, but the simulation on MPC is impossible.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the simulation of PRAM by MPC and the bounded-degree network is possible with the same number of processors, but the simulation is more expensive for MPCs.
we show that PRAMs can be simulated by MPCs in a non-uniform fashion with O(log n) slowdown and by bounded-degree processor networks with O((log n)^2) slowdown.

The main takeaway from our work is that

MPCs are more powerful than bounded-degree processor networks in the sense of deterministic simulation of idealized parallel machines, but they are less powerful in the probabilistic sense, as was shown by Upfal and Vigderson.
